docs.title: OntoBDC
docs.text:
OntoBDC is a Python CLI and semantic runtime for defining, discovering, validating, and executing capability-based workflows over structured data and semantic context.

It focuses on making workflows more predictable and auditable by combining explicit capability metadata, schema-driven inputs/outputs, and verification steps (e.g., checks, contracts, storage indexing) around execution.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: • Use Cases: documentation/use_case/README.md

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
1. Initialize a project context:
  2. ontobdc init
  3. Validate environment and configuration:
  4. ontobdc check
  5. Discover what is available:
  6. ontobdc list
  7. Execute a capability:
  8. ontobdc run <capability_id> [args]
  9. Manage the storage index:
  10. ontobdc storage
  11. ontobdc storage --local [path]
  12. ontobdc storage --remove <dataset_id>

docs.title: What OntoBDC Does
docs.text:
• Creates and maintains a per-project configuration in .__ontobdc__/config.yaml.
  • Runs pre-flight checks to reduce environment drift before execution.
  • Discovers installed capabilities and exposes them through a consistent CLI.
  • Executes capabilities using declared schemas and runtime strategies.
  • Maintains a storage index (.__ontobdc__/storage.rdf) that references dataset locations.
  • Supports workflows in domains that benefit from explicit contracts and auditability (e.g., BIM/openBIM, engineering data, compliance-oriented pipelines).

docs.title: Core Concepts (Mental Model)
docs.text:
• Project Context: the .__ontobdc__ folder that stores project state and metadata.
  • Capability: an executable unit with explicit metadata, inputs, and outputs.
  • Checks: deterministic validations to ensure the environment and prerequisites are correct before execution.
  • Storage Index: an RDF index that registers dataset locations and enables repeatable references.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: OntoBDC is under active development. The CLI is usable, but capabilities and workflows evolve quickly as the project expands its domain coverage and validation strategy.

docs.title: A3 Work Pipeline Sequence
docs.text:
This diagram illustrates the sequence of operations when executing the ontobdc a3 --work command. It shows how the concurrent workers, the physical package state evaluator, and the Sismic state machine interact to process each ETL package.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as CLI (ontobdc a3 --work)
    participant Core as work.main()
    participant Executor as ThreadPoolExecutor
    participant Worker as StateWorkerAdapter
    participant Handler as SismicA3TransitionHandlerAdapter
    participant Evaluator as StandardA3StateEvaluatorAdapter
    participant Sismic as Sismic Interpreter
    participant FS as File System (Package)

    CLI->>Core: Execute main()
    Core->>FS: list_package()
    FS-->>Core: List of LocalPackages

    loop For each Package
        Core->>Worker: Instantiate(package)
        Worker->>Handler: Instantiate(package)
        Handler->>Evaluator: Instantiate()
    end

    Core->>Executor: Submit workers (concurrently)

    par For each Submitted Worker
        Executor->>Worker: work()

        %% Determine initial state
        Worker->>Handler: get current_state
        Handler->>Evaluator: evaluate(package)
        Evaluator->>FS: Check existing files (reverse pipeline order)
        FS-->>Evaluator: Return most advanced file (e.g. raw.txt)
        Evaluator-->>Handler: Return A3EtlProcessState (e.g. RECEIVED)
        Handler-->>Worker: Return A3EtlProcessState

        %% Load and Initialize Machine
        Worker->>Worker: Load YAML Statechart
        Worker->>Sismic: Instantiate(statechart, context)
        Note right of Worker: Context injects handler<br/>and EtlProcessStatePort aliases
        Worker->>Sismic: Set initial state = current_state

        %% Execution Loop
        Worker->>Sismic: execute_once()
        loop while not Sismic.final
            Sismic->>Handler: evaluate guards (can_transit_to)
            Handler-->>Sismic: True/False

            opt If guard passes
                Sismic->>Handler: perform_state_transition(to_state)
                Note right of Handler: (Future) Execute Use Case
                Handler->>FS: Process & write new file (e.g. sanitized.txt)
                Sismic->>Handler: validate_state_transition()
                Handler-->>Sismic: True
            end

            Worker->>Sismic: execute_once()
            Worker->>Handler: get current_state
            Handler->>Evaluator: evaluate(package)
            Evaluator->>FS: Check files
            FS-->>Evaluator: Return new advanced file (e.g. sanitized.txt)
            Evaluator-->>Handler: Return new state (e.g. SANITIZED)
            Handler-->>Worker: Return new state

            opt If state did not change
                Worker-->>Executor: raise RuntimeError("State stuck")
            end
        end

        Worker-->>Executor: Return Success Result
    end

    Executor-->>Core: Return all results
    Core-->>CLI: message_box(Success)

docs.title: Three-Level Agent Architecture
docs.text: According to the project's architecture guidelines, the listed CLI commands act as orchestrators (L3 Use Cases) that modify business or environment states, utilizing: - L1 Capabilities: Discovery/read-only tools (e.g., data extraction via ontobdc run). - L2 Actions: Local transformation tools. - L3 Use Cases: Commands and flows that change the system state (e.g., init, storage add, dev commit).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This use case is responsible for initializing the OntoBDC configuration for a given project. It sets up the environment and creates the necessary configuration files, specifying the execution engine (e.g., venv or colab).

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User: Executes the CLI command to initialize the project.
  • System (OntoBDC): Creates and populates the local OntoBDC project configuration (.__ontobdc__/config.yaml), selecting and persisting the execution engine and default settings.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text:
• OntoBDC is installed.
  • The user is in the root directory of their project.

docs.title: Flow of Events
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc init.
  2. The system checks if the .__ontobdc__ folder and config.yaml exist.
  3. If they don't exist, the system generates them with default configurations.
  4. The system prompts the user or defaults to an engine (like venv).
  5. The project is marked as initialized and ready for execution.

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text: • The .__ontobdc__/config.yaml file is created and populated with valid initialization data.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This use case runs a series of infrastructure checks defined in the check module. It verifies dependencies, active environments, required engines, internet connection, and specific configurations for the project.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User: Wants to verify if their environment is ready.
  • System (OntoBDC): Internally calls this use case before running capabilities to ensure safety.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text: • The project must be initialized (.__ontobdc__/config.yaml exists).

docs.title: Flow of Events
docs.text:
1. The user or the system invokes ontobdc check.
  2. The system reads the global config.json and local config.yaml to determine which checks are enabled (auto: true).
  3. The system executes each check sequentially (e.g., is_venv_active, is_connected_to_internet, is_engine_installed).
  4. If --repair is passed, the system attempts to fix failing checks (e.g., installing Python dependencies).
  5. The system reports the final status of all checks.

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text:
• The user is informed about the environment's health.
  • If errors exist, the process halts, preventing runtime failures in capabilities.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This is the core use case of the OntoBDC stack. It executes a specific Capability (Query or Action) dynamically loaded from the available modules.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User: Wants to perform an operation (e.g., fetch a web link, extract data, transform schema).
  • System (OntoBDC): Resolves the requested Capability, validates CLI arguments against its schema, delegates execution to the appropriate strategy, and returns the produced output.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text:
• The project is initialized.
  • Infrastructure checks have passed.
  • The target capability is installed and available.

docs.title: Flow of Events
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc run <capability_id> [arguments].
  2. The system resolves the requested capability via CapabilityLoader .
  3. The system maps the provided CLI arguments to the input_schema defined in the capability's METADATA.
  4. The system delegates execution to the appropriate CliStrategy (e.g., CapabilityStrategy).
  5. The Capability executes, manipulating data, or interacting with the network.
  6. The system captures the output (e.g., a Knowledge Graph or JSON data) and presents it to the user.

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text:
• The capability's logic is fully executed.
  • Resulting data is returned or saved depending on the capability's design.

Cadeia exata que gera a mensagem - O ontobdc run monta a lista all_capabilities chamando get_all_capabilities(); ali ele percorre os pacotes retornados por load_capability_packages() e usa CapabilityLoader.load_from_package(pkg) para varrer/importar módulos e coletar classes com METADATA.id (run.py, loader.py). - Quando você passa --id, ele procura esse ID dentro de all_capabilities; se não achar, imprime exatamente “Capability Not Found …” e sai com erro (run.py).

Por que essa capability específica não entra em all_capabilities - A sua capability existe e define o ID exatamente como no erro (transformation_to_sanitized.py). - Só que o “descobridor” só varre os pacotes retornados por load_capability_packages(). E, quando não existe configuração, ele usa um default que não inclui ontobdc.a3.plugin (apenas ontobdc.module e ontobdc.storage.plugin) (util.py). - No seu .__ontobdc__/config.yaml não existe a seção capability: package: ... para adicionar ontobdc.a3.plugin, então ele cai nesse default (config.yaml).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This use case discovers and lists all available Capabilities (Query and Actions) registered in the current OntoBDC installation. It provides metadata such as ID, Version, Name, Description, and Schemas.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User: Wants to explore available tools and their usage schemas.
  • System (OntoBDC): Discovers installed Capabilities, extracts their metadata, and renders the result as Rich UI output or JSON.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text: • None (works globally or within an initialized project).

docs.title: Flow of Events
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc list (optionally with --json).
  2. The system scans all python packages and modules for classes inheriting from Capability (Query or Action).
  3. The system extracts the METADATA attribute from each discovered class.
  4. The system formats the output as Rich UI cards or JSON if requested.

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text: • The user sees a complete directory of available tools to use with ontobdc run.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This use case manages the local storage index for OntoBDC datasets. It allows the user to list registered datasets, initialize a local storage path, and remove datasets from the index.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User: Needs to manage local datasets and storage repositories.
  • System (OntoBDC): Interacts with storage adapters to manage the local storage index, enabling listing, adding, removing, and refreshing dataset resources.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text:
• The project is initialized.
  • The storage module dependencies (like datapackage, rocrate) are available.

docs.title: Flow of Events
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc storage (no arguments).
  2. The system checks whether a storage index exists (.__ontobdc__/storage.rdf).
  3. If the index does not exist, the system warns that no storage has been initialized and suggests ontobdc storage --local [path].
  4. If the index exists, the system parses it and prints the registered datasets.
  5. Optionally, the user runs ontobdc storage --local [path] to initialize/register a local storage path (default: project root when omitted).
  6. The system resolves the provided path (relative paths are resolved against the project root) and validates that it exists and is a directory.
  7. The system creates the storage index if needed, then registers the dataset location in the index and persists it to storage.rdf.
  8. The system ensures the dataset has the expected RO-Crate/ICDD structure (creating .__icdd__/payload/triples/ro-crate-metadata.json when missing).
  9. Optionally, the user runs ontobdc storage --remove <dataset_id> to remove a dataset.
  10. The system removes the dataset entry from the index, saves the updated index, and reports success (or warns if the dataset is not found).

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text: • The storage index is updated or displayed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This use case covers the developer-oriented command group exposed by ontobdc dev. It centralizes repository workflows such as enabling the dev tool, creating semantic commits, inspecting or creating branches, checking out branches, and persisting repository SSH key settings in the local project configuration.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User (Contributor/Developer): Needs to commit code or manage branches according to project rules.
  • System (OntoBDC): Provides developer utilities that enforce project conventions, validating configuration and invoking underlying Git operations when rules are satisfied.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text:
• The project is initialized.
  • The user is inside a Git repository for branch and commit operations.
  • The dev.tool flag is required for most developer commands and can be enabled from the CLI.

docs.title: Supported Commands
docs.text:
• ontobdc dev
  • ontobdc dev --help
  • ontobdc dev --enable-dev-tool
  • ontobdc dev commit "<message>"
  • ontobdc dev branch
  • ontobdc dev branch --create <name>
  • ontobdc dev checkout <name>
  • ontobdc dev repo --add-ssh-key <path>
  • ontobdc dev repo --rm-ssh-key

docs.title: Flow A - Enable the Dev Tool
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc dev --enable-dev-tool.
  2. The system verifies that the flag was passed alone.
  3. The system writes dev.tool: enabled to .__ontobdc__/config.yaml.
  4. The system confirms that developer commands are now enabled for the current project.

docs.title: Flow B - Create a Semantic Commit
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc dev commit "<message>".
  2. The system verifies that dev.tool is enabled.
  3. The system validates the provided commit message according to the project's semantic commit rules.
  4. If valid, the system delegates the operation to the commit script, which performs the repository commit workflow.
  5. If invalid, the system rejects the message and shows usage guidance.

docs.title: Flow C - Inspect or Create Branches
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc dev branch.
  2. The system verifies that dev.tool is enabled.
  3. The system delegates to the branch management script.
  4. The script lists repositories/submodules and reports branch-related Git status.
  5. Optionally, the user runs ontobdc dev branch --create <name>.
  6. The system creates and pushes the requested branch across the configured repositories.

docs.title: Flow D - Checkout an Existing Branch
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc dev checkout <name>.
  2. The system verifies that dev.tool is enabled.
  3. The system delegates to the branch script using checkout mode.
  4. The target branch is checked out across the participating repositories.

docs.title: Flow E - Persist Repository SSH Key Settings
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc dev repo --add-ssh-key <path>.
  2. The system verifies that dev.tool is enabled.
  3. The system writes the path to dev.repo.ssh.key_path in .__ontobdc__/config.yaml.
  4. Optionally, the user runs ontobdc dev repo --rm-ssh-key.
  5. The system removes the stored SSH key path from the local configuration.

docs.title: Alternative and Error Flows
docs.text:
1. If dev.tool is not enabled and the user runs a protected dev command, the system aborts and instructs the user to run ontobdc dev --enable-dev-tool.
  2. If --enable-dev-tool is combined with other arguments, the system rejects the call.
  3. If commit is called without a message, the system aborts and prints the correct usage.
  4. If repo is called without a supported option or with invalid arguments, the system aborts and prints the accepted syntax.
  5. If a branch or commit operation fails in the underlying Git scripts, the system propagates the failure to the user.

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text:
• The local project configuration may be updated with developer settings.
  • Commits and branch states may be changed in the target repositories.
  • The user receives guided feedback when a developer command is disabled or called incorrectly.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This use case covers the complete operational flow of the A3 module in OntoBDC. The command group ontobdc a3 is responsible for:

  • ingesting a text source into the A3 lifecycle area;
  • organizing the source as a deterministic package;
  • advancing the package through the A3 state machine;
  • generating intermediate artifacts for each processing stage;
  • validating the RDF output against SHACL; and
  • dispatching the final result as event.jsonld.

The current A3 pipeline is artifact-driven. A package advances physically according to the files found in its lifecycle directory, which also allows execution to resume from the most advanced completed step.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
• User: Wants to ingest a source and process it through the A3 extraction pipeline.
  • System (OntoBDC): Validates module availability, accepts the source, persists the package, evaluates package state from artifacts, executes the corresponding transformation capabilities, and reports success or failure.

docs.title: Pre-conditions
docs.text:
• The project is initialized.
  • The A3 extra is enabled in the current environment: ontobdc extra --enable a3.
  • The runtime environment can access the lifecycle directory used by A3.
  • When the parsed and validated stages are reached, the environment must also support:
  • network access to retrieve the ontology and SHACL shape;
  • the configured LLM CLI used by the parser capability; and
  • pyshacl installed as part of the A3 dependencies.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
• ontobdc a3
  • ontobdc a3 --help
  • ontobdc a3 -h

Displays the A3 help menu after verifying that the module is enabled.

docs.title: Ingestion
docs.text:
• ontobdc a3 --etl --source <file|url>

Creates or reuses a lifecycle package from the provided source and persists the original textual content as raw.txt.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text:
• ontobdc a3 --work

Scans all lifecycle packages and processes them concurrently, one worker per package, until each package reaches a final state or an error interrupts execution.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc a3 --etl --source <file|url>.
  2. The system verifies that the A3 module is enabled.
  3. The system validates that --source was provided.
  4. The system resolves a compatible extraction strategy for the source.
  5. The system extracts the source content.
  6. If the extracted resource is textual, the system normalizes it into an A3 raw text resource.
  7. The system computes a deterministic package identifier from the normalized content.
  8. The system writes raw.txt inside the lifecycle package directory.
  9. The system reports that the ETL start succeeded.
  10. The user runs ontobdc a3 --work.
  11. The system lists all packages in the lifecycle directory.
  12. The system creates one A3 worker per package and executes them concurrently.
  13. Each worker evaluates the package state by inspecting existing artifacts on disk.
  14. The worker initializes the A3 statechart from the current physical state.
  15. The worker repeatedly executes the next valid transition until the package reaches the final dispatched state.
  16. For each transition, the system resolves the capability whose identifier targets the destination state and executes it with the package as input.
  17. The system writes the artifact produced by that stage back into the same package directory.
  18. When all workers finish successfully, the system reports the final state of each processed package.

docs.title: State Sequence
docs.text:
The current canonical state sequence is:

undefined -> received -> sanitized -> parsed -> translated -> validated -> reasoned -> dispatched

docs.title: Physical State Rule
docs.text: The current state of a package is not inferred from metadata or a database record. It is derived from the files found in the package directory. The most advanced recognized artifact determines the package state.

docs.title: State Artifacts
docs.text: State Required artifact Meaning undefined none No known A3 artifact exists yet. received raw.txt Original extracted text was stored in the package. sanitized sanitized.txt Basic sanitization was completed. parsed parsed.json The LLM produced structured JSON validated by the guardrail. translated graph.ttl The structured JSON was converted into RDF/Turtle according to the SHACL shape. validated validated.txt The RDF graph conforms to SHACL and the validation report was persisted. reasoned reasoned.ttl A reasoning placeholder artifact was created from the graph. dispatched event.jsonld The package was emitted as a final event payload.

docs.title: received -> sanitized
docs.text:
• Input: raw.txt
  • Output: sanitized.txt
  • Behavior: performs a basic cleanup step, currently removing simple HTML tags from the raw text.

docs.title: sanitized -> parsed
docs.text:
• Input: sanitized.txt
  • Output: parsed.json
  • Supporting output on failure: err.json
  • Behavior:
  • downloads the ontology referenced by the guardrail shape URI;
  • reads the extraction prompt from ontology terms linked through peo:hasPrompt and peo:hasInstruction;
  • builds a constrained output schema from the SHACL-derived guardrail;
  • invokes the configured LLM CLI to extract structured data; and
  • validates the resulting JSON against required fields, types, cardinality, enums, patterns, and closed-shape constraints.

docs.title: parsed -> translated
docs.text:
• Input: parsed.json
  • Output: graph.ttl
  • Behavior:
  • downloads the target shape ontology;
  • reads sh:targetClass and each sh:property;
  • creates the subject URI from the parsed name;
  • converts scalar and array properties into RDF triples; and
  • normalizes enumerated values against sh:in before serialization.

docs.title: translated -> validated
docs.text:
• Input: graph.ttl
  • Output on success: validated.txt
  • Output on failure: err.json
  • Behavior:
  • downloads the SHACL document;
  • validates the RDF graph with pyshacl; and
  • persists the SHACL validation report when the graph conforms.

docs.title: validated -> reasoned
docs.text:
• Input: graph.ttl
  • Output: reasoned.ttl
  • Behavior: creates a reasoning placeholder by copying graph.ttl into reasoned.ttl. No inference engine is executed yet.

docs.title: reasoned -> dispatched
docs.text:
• Input: graph.ttl
  • Output: event.jsonld
  • Behavior:
  • reads the RDF graph;
  • rewrites the primary subject as an event identifier;
  • serializes the result as JSON-LD.

The event identifier follows this pattern:

urn:<shape_name_snake_case>:event/<package>/<timestamp>

For the current job offer flow, the target shape is JobOfferShape, which yields event identifiers such as:

urn:job_offer:event/<package>/<timestamp>

docs.title: Lifecycle Directory
docs.text: A3 stores packages inside the lifecycle dataset resolved by the current OntoBDC configuration. In practice, this corresponds to the A3 payload lifecycle area under the local configuration directory.

docs.title: Package Identity
docs.text: The ingestion step computes the package identifier from normalized raw text. The same text therefore maps to the same package directory, which helps avoid duplicate lifecycle roots for identical content.

docs.title: Resume Semantics
docs.text:
ontobdc a3 --work resumes from the most advanced artifact already present in each package. For example:

  • if only raw.txt exists, the package starts at received;
  • if parsed.json already exists, the package resumes from parsed;
  • if event.jsonld exists, the package is already in its final state.

This also means stale artifacts can change the state perceived by the worker and must be considered during troubleshooting.

docs.title: A3 Not Enabled
docs.text:
1. The user runs any ontobdc a3 command.
  2. The system detects that the A3 extra is not enabled.
  3. The system aborts and instructs the user to run ontobdc extra --enable a3.

docs.title: Missing --source
docs.text:
1. The user runs ontobdc a3 --etl without --source.
  2. The system rejects the call.
  3. The system prints usage guidance with an example.

docs.title: Unsupported Extracted Resource
docs.text:
1. The user provides a source that does not resolve to a text resource.
  2. The system aborts the ETL ingestion.
  3. The current implementation raises NotImplementedError, because only textual resources are supported by A3 ingestion.

docs.title: Invalid Package Transition
docs.text:
1. A worker attempts to run a transition that does not match the package's current physical state.
  2. The target capability rejects the execution.
  3. The worker fails and reports the package-specific exception.

docs.title: Parsing Failure
docs.text:
1. The parser capability cannot proceed, the LLM execution fails, or the generated JSON violates the guardrail.
  2. The system writes err.json with the current state and error message.
  3. The worker aborts processing for that package.

docs.title: SHACL Validation Failure
docs.text:
1. The translated RDF graph does not conform to the SHACL shape.
  2. The system writes err.json with the current state and validation error.
  3. The worker aborts processing for that package.

docs.title: Stuck State
docs.text:
1. A worker executes the state machine but no physical transition occurs.
  2. The system raises a runtime error indicating that the package is stuck at the current state.
  3. The user must inspect the package artifacts and the generated error details.

docs.title: Post-conditions
docs.text:
• After --etl, the source has been materialized as a lifecycle package containing at least raw.txt.
  • After a successful --work, each processed package reaches dispatched.
  • A successfully completed package contains the full trace of intermediate artifacts generated by the pipeline.
  • The final exported event is stored as event.jsonld.
  • If a stage fails, the package preserves its intermediate artifacts and may also contain err.json for diagnosis.
